content:
In France, the social security system covers all prenatal and postnatal care in public hospitals at no cost. Working women are also guaranteed 16 weeks of maternity leave, with daily compensation ranging from approximately €9.29 to €84.90, depending on their prior earnings. During pregnancy and the period surrounding childbirth, financial circumstances remain largely the same as before - lower-income families continue to face economic hardships, while higher-income families maintain their financial stability.

However, when it comes to the support available for new mothers, the system falls noticeably short. Paternity leave is limited to just 11 days, which is barely adequate for mothers to physically recover from giving birth. This means new mothers must cope with the relentless and demanding responsibilities of caring for a newborn while still healing. They are also tasked with finding suitable childcare options, despite the fact that government-provided programs are insufficient, particularly in the Paris area.

Childcare costs vary considerably. Public daycare centers can cost lower-income families as little as €1,000 per year, but availability is severely limited, with only one spot available for every eight children. As a result, many families are forced to turn to private alternatives, such as independent childminders or in-home caregivers, to meet their childcare needs.

Any other questions?
